tool.name: XPS peak finding
tool.description: in a NeXus spectrum, written back as NXfit/NXpeak

param.name: input_nxs
param.label: XPS spectrum (NeXus/HDF5)
param.help: An already-converted NeXus file (for example NXxps) with a resolvable default NXdata group holding energy vs. intensity.

param.label: Required prominence of peaks
param.help: How far a peak must stand out from the surrounding baseline, in the intensity units of the spectrum. Left empty, scipy applies no prominence filter and typically returns hundreds of peaks. For a survey spectrum in counts per second, 10000 is a reasonable starting point.

param.label: Minimal horizontal distance between peaks
param.help: In data points, not energy units. Smaller peaks within this distance of a larger one are discarded. Try 20 for a survey spectrum.

param.label: Required absolute height of peaks
param.help: Minimum intensity a peak must reach, in the intensity units of the spectrum. Unlike prominence this ignores the local baseline, so it is mostly useful for picking out only the strongest lines.

tool.help:
**What it does**
Finds peaks in an X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) spectrum stored in a NeXus/HDF5 file, and writes the detected peaks back into a copy of that file as a standard ``NXfit`` group.
The tool reads the spectrum from the file's *default* ``NXdata`` group (energy vs. intensity), runs ``scipy.signal.find_peaks`` over the intensity, and appends one ``NXpeak`` group per detected peak. The input dataset is never modified.
This is the peak-finding step of the NOMAD ↔ Galaxy XPS demonstrator.
-----
**Inputs**
A NeXus file that has already been converted from a vendor format - for example the output of ``pynxtools-xps``. It must contain an ``NXentry`` with a resolvable default ``NXdata`` group. Upload it to Galaxy as datatype ``h5``.
-----
**Peak detection parameters**
All three are optional and map directly onto ``scipy.signal.find_peaks``. Leave them all empty and you get every local maximum in the spectrum, which is rarely what you want - ``prominence`` is usually the most useful single knob.
The right values depend on the intensity scale of your data. For the survey spectrum used in the tool's tests (counts per second), ``prominence = 10000`` with ``distance = 20`` picks out the six main lines.
-----
**Outputs**
**Annotated NeXus** - a copy of the input with the peaks added under ``/<entry>/fit``. For each detected peak *i*:
``/<entry>/fit`` - ``@NX_class = NXfit``, holds a ``label`` describing how the peaks were found.
``/<entry>/fit/peak_<i>`` - ``@NX_class = NXpeak``, holds a ``label``.
``/<entry>/fit/peak_<i>/data`` - ``@NX_class = NXdata``, holds ``position`` (with ``@units`` taken from the spectrum's energy axis, typically ``eV``) and ``intensity`` (with ``@units`` taken from the signal, e.g. ``counts_per_second``).
**Peak table** - tabular, with ``peak_id``, ``position`` and ``intensity`` columns, ready for Galaxy's filtering, joining and plotting tools.
**Peaks (JSON)** - the same peaks as a JSON list of ``{"position": ..., "intensity": ...}`` objects.
-----
